speaker: Karri Saarinen
title: Inside Linear: Building with taste, craft, and focus | Karri Saarinen
question: In B2B collaboration software, how do high-craft product teams avoid letting a high quality bar stall shipping?
guest: On product craft, it starts with hiring people who care about it. We see that cooperation only happens if people actually use the product, and if there's friction or little paper cuts, it gets annoying to use. There are definitely trade-offs on timelines—sometimes before a launch we notice something doesn't feel right and push it back by days, not redoing everything. At the same time, we don't spend tons of time upfront designing and polishing a new feature perfectly, because we believe that once you start building it, you realize how it should actually work and be better. So we tell teams to put it in the app within the first week and ship it to production visible only to us internally. Next, we ask a small group of customers to opt into a beta. In those stages, the experience can be a little janky because we explicitly say it's unfinished and want early feedback. Once we get to the full general release, that's when we apply strict attention to the polish and craft.

points.core: Teams avoid excessive upfront polishing because real design flaws emerge during active building.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
High-craft teams like Linear, Figma, Slack, and Notion generally resolve this tension by narrowing scope rather than lowering the bar. They ship a smaller thing that is fully polished instead of a broad thing that is half-finished, so quality constrains what gets built, not when it ships.

A few practices recur. They fix time and flex scope: short cycles or firm deadlines force cutting features, not finish. They keep teams small with a single directly responsible owner, so quality decisions get made quickly by someone with taste instead of by committee review. They dogfood heavily and release in stages (internal use, then private beta with select customers, then general availability), so real feedback arrives early while the public release still feels finished. They distinguish reversible from irreversible decisions, moving fast on the former and reserving deliberation for core interactions, data models, and APIs that are costly to change. And they treat polish as continuous work, through recurring "quality weeks," bug-fix rotations, or zero-bug policies, so that shipping something is the start of refinement, not a final exam it must pass first.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
High-craft B2B collaboration teams avoid stalling by cutting scope ruthlessly rather than lowering execution quality: instead of shipping a broad, half-baked release, they narrow v1 to the smallest cohesive workflow and finish that slice completely. They separate learning from public launch through heavy internal dogfooding, feature flags, and opt-in customer betas, validating messy multi-user dynamics in real work before locking down final details.

Just as importantly, they amortize craft through shared infrastructure—opinionated design systems, accessible keyboard and interaction primitives, and fast optimistic-update architectures—so responsiveness and visual consistency are inherited by default rather than rebuilt from scratch on every project. Designers and engineers also collaborate directly in live builds instead of passing static mocks across handoffs, resolving feel and edge cases in code as they go and timeboxing focused polish bashes right before widening rollout. Finally, they apply the quality bar asymmetrically, investing obsessive care in high-frequency daily collaboration loops while keeping low-traffic administrative surfaces straightforward and pragmatic.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
High-craft teams like Linear, Figma and Notion keep quality high by cutting scope instead of polish. They ship a smaller version that is excellent, not a full version that is mediocre. A narrow feature with one polished workflow goes out, and the rest follows in later releases.

They also separate shipping from releasing. Work merges early behind feature flags. The team uses it internally first, then opens it to design partners or beta workspaces. That gives real-world feedback while the public bar stays intact. Fixed-length cycles or appetite-based bets, as in Shape Up, cap how long anything can be polished, so perfectionism hits a deadline.

They decide which kind of quality matters where. Hard-to-reverse things like data models, permissions, sync behavior and public APIs get rigorous design up front. UI details and copy are treated as easy to iterate. Bugs and rough edges are handled continuously, through zero-bug policies, dedicated polish weeks or quality rotations, so they don't pile up into a release blocker. Clear ownership gives one person authority to call "good enough to ship," which avoids debating quality by committee.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
High-craft B2B collaboration teams protect both quality and velocity by cutting scope rather than cutting polish. Instead of building sprawling features and debating every edge case before launch, they narrow each release to a small, coherent workflow that feels complete on its own. Fixed timeboxes, such as short cycles or appetites, force those scope trade-offs early so perfectionism cannot stretch a project indefinitely.

They also make quality inexpensive to maintain by investing in strong design systems, shared interaction primitives, and opinionated defaults, so teams do not have to reinvent basic craft on every screen. Rather than waiting for theoretical perfection, they rely on progressive exposure: dogfooding internally in their own daily work, shipping behind feature flags to small customer cohorts, and learning from real collaboration friction before general availability. Finally, they draw a clear line between true launch blockers—like data integrity, speed, and core usability—and fast-follow refinements, reserving dedicated post-launch time for polish so shipping early never feels like abandoning quality.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
High-craft teams keep shipping by narrowing each release to the smallest workflow customers can use end to end. They agree up front on what must work at launch and what can follow. In a shared workspace, that might mean getting permissions, sync, and recovery right before adding more notification settings or polishing an animation.

They review working software early, put it in the hands of a few customer teams, and expand access as they see how it holds up in real work. If a release misses the bar, they cut scope or keep it in beta. They give deferred improvements an owner and revisit them using customer feedback and usage data. Small releases make quality easier to judge because the team can see where people get stuck and fix it while the context is fresh.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
High-craft teams keep the quality bar high by narrowing what they promise in each release. They choose one workflow a customer can complete end to end and agree up front on what would make it ready to ship. For example, a team might launch document sharing with two well-tested roles, then add custom roles later. A permission leak blocks the release. A request for a third role can wait.

They put that smaller release in the hands of a few customer teams early and watch people use it together. If recipients routinely need help opening a shared document, that friction deserves attention before a wider rollout. If people complete the workflow confidently, the team can ship more broadly and let real use guide the next round of polish.
